topicA.name: B2B Paid Search and Rising Ad Costs

resources.headline: Same B2B Google Ads Keywords Cost About 21% More, Agency Data Shows via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
resources.fullText: To determine how much more the same non-branded Google Ads keywords cost 14 B2B advertisers per click during the months of April through September compared to the same time period last year, Grey Matter reviewed their Google Ads Search campaigns. According to the agency report by Grey Matter issued in October, there was an increase of about 21% in cost-per-click (CPC) for the same keywords used by these 14 B2B advertisers, after accounting for changes in their spending, ad position and Quality Score. The report gives a likely range of 1% to 44% for that figure. It is based on client Google Ads Search campaign data only, so it does not include Performance Max, Shopping or Display campaigns. All 14 come from the agency’s client base, and its search team runs SEO and paid search programs for B2B companies. Andy Hendricks, Grey Matter’s head of search, writes that he wanted to isolate what portion of the overall price change all advertisers experienced versus what portion was due to actions taken by each advertiser individually. Most available CPC benchmarks, such as published averages, do not account for this differentiation and simply provide an overall average CPC. How The Report Measured The Same Click Grey Matter excluded broad match keywords since the searches they get matched to can change over time; keywords within Maximize Clicks campaigns also do not fit into the analysis. Brand and competitor keywords were also excluded from the overall estimate. Grey Matter’s analysis is based on tracking 1,349 non-brand keywords, each within one account, for six quarters (April 2025 to September 2026). The year-over-year comparison covers April through September 2026 versus those months a year prior. The headline estimate was derived from a regression model using data from all 14 advertisers in the report which controlled for campaign spend, impression share lost to budget, top-of-page position, and Quality Score. Every advertiser was given equal weight regardless of how much it spends. With no controls applied, the same keywords cost 29% more year over year. Adding the two spend-related controls lowered that to 22%, and position and Quality Score took it to 21%. A second estimation technique used in this analysis was a keyword price index. This measure covered 11 advertisers who had sufficient matching keywords from quarter to quarter. Higher Spend Went With Higher CPCs On The Same Keywords The report’s regression ties every 10% increase in campaign spend to about 1.4% higher CPCs, on top of the market increase, or roughly 11% for doubled spend. The report doesn’t give a likely range for that figure. The most extreme case in the sample nearly quadrupled its non-brand Search spend year over year, and its same-keyword CPCs rose 132%. The report says that advertiser’s brand keywords, on a flat budget, rose about 4% year over year in the third quarter. The report sees a correlation between this pattern and automated bidding. It explains that a campaign using a strategy like Maximize Conversions spends a bigger budget by entering auctions it previously skipped, including higher positions, more competitive searches, and pricier times of day. What The 11 Advertisers Paid Overall For the 11 advertisers covered by the keyword price index, the overall year-over-year increase in average non-brand CPC was 36%, including the advertisers’ own choices. Of that, 22 points were attributed to the market, and three additional points were attributed to increased spending. There was a three-point deduction due to various types of keyword, match type and bid strategy changes, leaving 14 points that the report’s first three parts don’t explain. Grey Matter illustrates that breakdown in the chart below. Source: Grey Matter, Same Click, Higher Price, October 2026 (cropped). The majority of those 14 points occurred at a few of the advertisers who saw an approximate doubling of their CPCs, which the report said probably represented competition in their respective categories. Actual CPC changes ranged from a 30% decrease to a 121% increase. Ten of the 11 paid more for the same keywords, and nine paid more overall. One advertiser kept its spending flat and saw the same keywords rise by 20%. After shifting some of its budget to pricier phrase-match keywords, its overall CPC increased by 40%. How Firm The 21% Is With only 14 advertisers in this report, the likely range for the 21% estimate is wide. When the biggest spender is removed from the report’s data, the estimate drops to around 17%, and its likely range of -2% to +40% includes zero. When broad match keywords are included, the estimate rises to around 31%. According to Hendricks, compared with a year ago, that same click most likely costs about 20% more currently, and the true figure “could be meaningfully higher or lower”. The report calls its findings correlation (and not proven causation). There are no references on the report page or in the PDF to the industries or markets of the advertisers used in the report, nor their currency. The report doesn’t provide any conversion rate or cost per lead information; so, it can’t show whether these advertisers saw better or worse results along with higher CPCs. Jyll Saskin Gales argued in an April column for Search Engine Journal (SEJ) that under Smart Bidding, a high CPC is often a sign of a healthy account, and that accounts should be evaluated based on CPA or ROAS. Google’s Own CPC Figure Measures Something Else Alphabet’s third-quarter 10-Q reports that cost-per-click on Google Search & other properties rose 4% year over year in the quarter. Alphabet has defined this metric as click-driven revenue divided by total paid clicks and has cited several factors such as changes in the devices users access the internet on, geography, advertiser spending, and product mix as variables that affect it. The metric is based on paid clicks through Google Search properties and other platforms owned by Alphabet, so it will track with the
keyNotes: Surprisingly, the cost for businesses to advertise on Google using specific search terms (called "keywords") has gone up significantly. A study found that for 14 business-to-business (B2B) companies, the cost they pay each time someone clicks their ad (called "cost-per-click" or CPC) increased by about 21% for the same keywords compared to last year.

One big reason for these rising ad costs is simply spending more money. The study showed that for every 10% more a company spent on their ad campaigns, their cost-per-click went up by about 1.4% on top of the general market increase.

Some companies saw much larger increases; for instance, one advertiser who nearly quadrupled their ad spending saw their cost-per-click for the same keywords jump by a massive 132%. This suggests that automated systems that bid for ads might be pushing costs higher by entering more expensive ad slots.

While the overall market generally pushed ad costs up, individual company choices also played a role. For some advertisers, 22 percentage points of their average 36% cost-per-click increase were due to the market, but another 3 percentage points were because they increased their own spending.

It's crucial to remember that paying more for ads doesn't automatically mean better results. The study didn't look at whether these companies actually got more sales or leads for their higher ad spending, so we don't know if the increased cost was worth it.
resources.question: The study found that while ad costs went up by as much as 132% for some, it didn't track whether these higher costs actually led to more sales or customers for the businesses. If you were managing a budget for your own business, how would you decide if paying significantly more for something (like advertising or any other business expense) was actually a good investment, especially if you couldn't directly see the return?

resources.headline: 72% Of Worker’s Say Their AI Skills Are Untested – Here’s How PPC Managers Prove Theirs via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
resources.fullText: If you manage Google Ads accounts, being “good” with AI is expected, but employers probably never checked (or didn’t know how to check) if you are. Being able to show your judgment is a career must if you can, and a risk if you can’t. New research from CodeSignal surveyed 1,000 U.S. employees and 1,000 U.S. people managers about AI readiness, and two numbers sit side by side in the results. 72% of workers surveyed say their AI skills have never been formally evaluated, yet 69% of managers call AI ability a major or moderate factor in hiring. Indicating that employers are hiring for a skill they mostly don’t measure. I sent CodeSignal 15 questions about how solid those numbers are and what practitioners should do about them. The written answers were more candid than I expected, including on the obvious conflict of interest of an assessment vendor concluding that nobody assesses anything. Here’s what holds up, what needs a footnote, and what it means for people who run paid search for a living. Who CodeSignal Actually Surveyed Start with what this survey is and isn’t. CodeSignal commissioned two online surveys through Pollfish in September 2026, and both samples were entirely U.S.-based. The company defined knowledge workers by the work they do rather than by job title, meaning people whose jobs run mainly on computers and digital tools. It also didn’t screen out people who skip AI. 12% said they never use it at work. CodeSignal reports that roles where AI use is required or expected “jumped 78%.” I asked whether that meant percentage points. It doesn’t. It’s a relative increase, self-reported by employees about their own roles, measured across each person’s time in their current job. When respondents started those jobs, 9.4% said AI use was required or expected of them. Today, 16.7% say so. That’s nearly double. It’s also fewer than one in five. Paid search people are probably well past that curve already, since automated bidding has been Google’s default recommendation for years. So, the useful question for our field is whether anyone can tell who is using AI well. See also: From T-Shaped To M-Shaped: The PPC Career Evolution Nobody Is Talking About The Training Happens, Then It Doesn’t Stick 62% of employees told CodeSignal they received employer training on how to use AI at work. Only 35% said employer training is where they built the AI skills they actually use. I asked whether most of that training simply wasn’t about AI, or whether workers weren’t counting it. CodeSignal said neither. The training was specifically about using AI at work, and the company reads the gap as a sign that it wasn’t substantial or specific enough to apply on the job. The follow-up number is worse. Only about one in four trained workers said they can apply most or all of their employer’s AI training. The other 74% apply some, very little, or none of it. Run that against the full sample and roughly 46% of all workers got AI training they can’t fully use. When CodeSignal asked what gets in the way, employees named lack of time, training that doesn’t fit their role, and lack of access to relevant training. So, where are people learning? The question allowed multiple answers, which is why the figures don’t add up to 100. Free resources people found on their own led at 46%, followed by trial and error on the job at 39%, and employer training at 35%. Colleagues came in at 22%, and courses people paid for themselves at 12%. Tigran Sloyan, CodeSignal’s co-founder and CEO, said, “Companies are buying AI courses or building their own, but if most workers are going elsewhere to learn, you have to wonder if that training is actually helping.” Paid search has worked this way for a long time. Plenty of PPC managers learned bidding by watching their own accounts and reading practitioners on LinkedIn and X. What has changed is that the thing they now learn by trial and error is the ad platform’s own AI, and each error is paid for out of a client’s budget. AI Didn’t Create The Measurement Problem, It Exposed It 72% of workers say their AI skills have never been formally evaluated, but 66% say the same about their skills in general. That’s a six-point gap. I asked CodeSignal whether the real story is that companies don’t assess much of anything, and AI just makes that visible. The answer began with “Yes, exactly.” Companies have long made people decisions on proxies such as resumes, job titles, tenure, and manager impressions. CodeSignal’s argument is that those were always weak signals, and they get costly when roles shift in months. More than six in ten managers in the survey said they make people decisions based on assumptions rather than reliable data. This bothers me more in paid media than almost anywhere else. We measure campaigns to the decimal point. We argue about attribution windows, incrementality tests, and conversion lag. Then we judge the people running those campaigns with a once-a-year “meets expectations.” For a discipline built on measurement, that’s a strange double standard, and AI is making it harder to defend. CodeSignal says the hiring side already shows the strain. When AI fluency is a criterion nobody has measured, people get judged on what’s easy to see, such as who is most visible or sounds most confident, instead of on the quality of their work. Anyone who has sat through an agency pitch knows how that plays out. The person who says the automation will figure it out can sound more fluent than the person who spent the afternoon reading search terms and adding negatives. Only one of them is protecting the budget. “A resume is a story someone tells about their skills,” Sloyan said. “The work is the proof. Right now, most companies are making their biggest decisions about people based on the story.” See also: PPC Automation Layering: How Smart Advertisers Combine Automation With Strategy What AI Fluency Means When You Run PPC I asked CodeSignal to separate “AI fluency” from AI literacy and prompt-writ
keyNotes: Even though most managers (69%) consider AI ability important when hiring, a large majority of workers (72%) say their AI skills have never been officially checked or tested. This means companies are often looking for a skill they don't actually measure.

Many companies offer training on how to use AI (62% of employees received it), but a surprising number of workers (only 35%) found that training actually helped them build the AI skills they use daily. This suggests much of the training isn't practical enough.
When employer training isn't cutting it, most people learn AI on their own through free online resources (46%) or by simply trying things out and learning from mistakes on the job (39%).

The problem of not testing AI skills isn't new; it highlights a bigger issue where 66% of workers say their skills *in general* are rarely formally evaluated. Companies often make important decisions about people based on things like resumes or how confident someone sounds, rather than actual proof of their work.

This lack of proper skill assessment can be costly, especially in areas like online advertising where mistakes made by AI (which people are supposed to manage) directly spend a client's money. It means companies might be judging people on how they *sound* rather than how well they *protect* the budget.
resources.question: The article points out that many companies rely on resumes and impressions rather than actual skill tests, especially with new technologies like AI. If you were to truly measure the practical skills needed for success in your own role or team, what specific, hands-on tasks would you use to prove someone's ability, and how might that differ from how skills are typically assessed today?

resources.headline: AI Bot Management: Why SEOs Need More Than Block Lists via @sejournal, @chrisgreenseo
resources.fullText: For years, bot management in SEO was relatively straightforward. You either allowed crawlers to access your website or blocked them. That model was never perfect, but it was generally sufficient for what we needed. Image from author, November 2026 AI search has made that approach increasingly inadequate. Today, websites are accessed by traditional search crawlers, AI training crawlers, retrieval bots, user-initiated fetches, and autonomous agents. These serve very different purposes, yet we regularly lump them together under the term “AI bots.” Blocking a crawler used for model training has different consequences from blocking one retrieving content for search answers – this distinction really matters! Robots.txt remains useful, but as it’s voluntary actual enforcement happens through CDNs, web application firewalls and bot mitigation services, which can contradict your robots.txt rules without the SEO team even knowing. Image from author, November 2026 Agents complicate matters further. They can browse websites like real users, trigger analytics tracking, and become increasingly difficult to distinguish from human visitors. Block an agent performing a product comparison, and you might not simply lose a ranking. You could disappear from the answer entirely. My argument is that we need to move from block lists to deliberate bot policies. Policies that consider who’s accessing our content, why they’re doing it and the consequences of allowing or blocking them. These decisions increasingly involve SEO, engineering, security, legal, and commercial teams. They need to be coordinated, consistently enforced and regularly reviewed. Image from author, November 2026 I’ve covered these challenges, their implications, and some practical approaches in my GEO Elite presentation. Hope you find it useful: More Resources: Complete Crawler List For AI User-Agents [Dec 2025] AI Bots Keep Overloading Servers. Should Website Owners Keep Paying? Web Almanac Data Reveals CMS Plugins Are Setting Technical SEO Standards (Not SEOs) This post was originally published on AI Search Marketing with Chris Green. Featured Image: Andrey Suslov/Shutterstock Category SEO Technical SEO
keyNotes: It turns out that simply blocking or allowing website visitors, which used to be enough, is no longer effective because new AI technologies mean many different types of automated programs (called "bots") are visiting your site for various reasons.

Blocking an automated program (a "bot") that's gathering information to train an AI model has a completely different impact than blocking one that's trying to find content for a search answer, and making the wrong choice could mean your content disappears from search results.

Even if you tell automated programs (bots) what they can and cannot do on your website using a standard file, other security systems might secretly override those instructions without your team ever knowing.

Some advanced AI programs, called "agents," can browse websites just like a human user, making it very hard to tell them apart from real visitors and potentially causing you to lose visibility if you block them.

Instead of just having a list of automated programs (bots) to block, businesses now need a detailed plan that considers who is visiting their site, why, and what happens if they are allowed or blocked, requiring different teams to work together.
resources.question: The article suggests that managing who accesses your website now requires "deliberate bot policies" involving many different departments like engineering, security, and legal. If you think about your own company's website, who would need to be involved in deciding which automated programs (bots) are allowed to visit and why?

topicB.name: Account-Based Marketing and B2B Sales Enablement

resources.headline: Seismic Research Shows Sellers Play A Bigger Role In High-Stakes Decisions
resources.fullText: Seismic's research found that most B2B leaders trust human guidance over AI-generated content, suggesting sellers play a bigger role in high-stakes decisions.
keyNotes: Surprisingly, a study by Seismic found that most business leaders (the people making big decisions for companies) trust advice from real people more than information created by artificial intelligence.

This means that when businesses are making really important choices, the person selling a product or service (often called a "seller") has a much bigger and more influential role than you might expect.
The research specifically pointed out that "B2B leaders" value human guidance most for "high-stakes decisions," which are critical choices with significant consequences for a business.

So, even in today's tech-driven world, the human connection and personal advice from a salesperson are still considered more trustworthy for crucial business decisions than anything an AI can generate.
resources.question: The research highlights that business leaders trust human advice more than AI for "high-stakes decisions." Thinking about your own work or personal life, how do you determine when a decision is "high-stakes," and what kind of human guidance do you seek out versus relying on automated information for those critical moments?

resources.headline: Plain Language Is A Total Experience Imperative
resources.fullText: < Featured Blogs Home > Featured Blogs > Plain Language Is A Total Experience Imperative Plain Language Is A Total Experience Imperative Have you ever read a communication three times and still had no idea what it was trying to tell you? Maybe it was an explanation of benefits from your health insurer, a letter from your bank about a fee change, an order update from a retailer, or a notice from a government agency. When this happens, we sometimes blame ourselves. Why don’t I understand this? I have news: The problem isn’t you. Organizations routinely make customers work too hard to understand information. And it turns out that the resulting confusion and other negative feelings this creates damages the customer experience, customer loyalty, and brand perception. At Forrester, we study dozens of drivers that influence brand experience (BX) and customer experience (CX), two dimensions of a brand’s total experience. “Communicates with me using plain language” is among the top drivers of total experience for auto manufacturers, banks, health insurers, hotels, investment firms, and retailers. Yet in these industries, fewer than two-thirds — and in some cases, fewer than half — of customers say that brands communicate in plain language. How To Communicate In Plain Language Plain language doesn’t only benefit people with limited English proficiency, lower reading levels, or learning disabilities. It helps all customers understand what they need to know, feel confident about what to do next, and leave an interaction with a more positive impression of your brand. In our new report, Communicate In Plain Language To Improve Your Total Experience, we identify six proven practices for communicating more clearly. They include: Avoid jargon (no, really) and scale plain language alternatives through your design system. Think your brand already does this? Our data shows that it probably doesn’t. Replace technical, legal, and internal jargon terminology with words your audience can understand. When technical terms are unavoidable, explain them using simple definitions, examples, or analogies. Scale the use of plain language alternatives for frequently used jargon by documenting words to use and avoid or “dos” and “don’ts” in your organization’s design system. When using generative AI to create content, always require human review before publication to ensure that it’s accurate, clear, and inclusive. Apply information design best practices. The way you structure and present content matters as much as the words themselves. Use descriptive headings, concise paragraphs, lists, white space, and progressive disclosure to help customers find and understand what matters most. Apply visual emphasis (such as bolding content) selectively. Ensure text is easy to read by meeting accessibility requirements for color contrast and font size and making sure that text size scales based on user-defined settings. See What Plain Language Looks Like In Practice Read Communicate In Plain Language To Improve Your Total Experience to explore all six best practices, understand why plain language has such an important influence on total experience, and see dozens of examples of how brands across industries communicate clearly in the moments that matter most.
